ANOMALIE RESIDUE E ALTERAZIONI DELLA CURVATURA DEL FUSTO ➰

Questa sezione raggruppa difetti acquisiti da trauma meccanico (annodamento) e anomalie congenite che alterano la geometria trasversale o la curvatura del fusto, influenzandone la pettinabilità e l'aspetto estetico senza necessariamente indurre fragilità da frattura.

1. Triconodòsi (Capello Annodato / Trichonodosis)

Definizione:
Anomalia esclusivamente acquisita caratterizzata dalla formazione di veri e propri nodi lungo il fusto (single-strand knots). A livello della spira del nodo, la tensione meccanica causa lo sfaldamento della cuticola con esposizione e sfilacciamento della corteccia.
Patogenesi e Biomeccanica:
Deriva da traumi meccanici ripetuti (spazzolatura aggressiva, frizione). La sezione trasversale fortemente appiattita o ellittica riduce il momento d'inerzia alla torsione (ossia la resistenza strutturale del capello ad avvitarsi su se stesso), favorendo l'arricciamento autogeno e l'annodamento ("effetto molla").
Fattori di Rischio:
Prevalente in chi ha capelli ricci, crespi o molto fini (etnia africana o capelli caucasici ricci). Raramente spontanea in capelli estremamente lunghi e trascurati.

2. Sindrome dei Capelli Impettinabili (Uncombable Hair Syndrome - UHS)

Quadro clinico pediatrico correlato al segno microscopico dei Pili trianguli et canaliculi (fusti a sezione triangolare con una scanalatura longitudinale), con graduale risoluzione spontanea durante la pubertà.

Eziologia Molecolare e Cascata Biochimica UHS

Pathway Genetico

Patologia genetica ad eredità autosomica recessiva legata a mutazioni nel complesso di cheratinizzazione follicolare: PADI3, TGM3, TCHH e SULT2B1.

Fase 1: Deimina della Tricoialina
PADI3 → TCHH
La peptidilarginina deiminasi 3 (PADI3) deimina la tricoialina (TCHH), permettendone il legame con i filamenti di cheratina.
↓
Fase 2: Legami Crociati Isopeptidici
TGM3 (Transglutaminasi 3)
Catalizza i legami crociati isopeptidici stabili per il consolidamento strutturale.
↓
Esito Patologico
Cheratinizzazione Prematura IRS
Il difetto dell'asse provoca la cheratinizzazione prematura della guaina epiteliale interna (IRS - Inner Root Sheath), deformatrice e rigidificante sul fusto malleabile.

Correlato Clinico: Capelli secchi, disordinati e proiettati verso l'esterno, impossibili da appiattire ma privi di un significativo incremento della fragilità alla trazione.

3. Capelli Lanosi (Woolly Hair)

Morfologia e Diagnosi Differenziale:
Fusti con sezione ovoidale/appiattita, caratterizzati da torsioni assiali strette e curvature irregolari. Rispetto ai Pili Torti (torsioni di 180° lungo l'asse longitudinale), le torsioni si presentano meno strutturate e la resistenza meccanica del capello è ampiamente conservata.
Fisiopatologia:
Marcata riduzione della fase anagen (fase di crescita attiva, con lunghezza massima del capello spesso < 5 cm). L'impossibilità di pettinaggio è legata alla densità spaziale delle micro-curvature e non a frattura del fusto.
Variante ClinicaEreditarietà & GeneticaCaratteristiche Patologiche & Associazioni
Ereditaria (Generalizzata)Autosomica Dominante o RecessivaCoinvolge l'intero cuoio capelluto. Le forme recessive sono marcatore di sindromi cardio-cutanee gravemente invalidanti (es. Sindrome di Naxos o di Carvajal per mutazioni nei geni desmosomiali JUP o DSP).
Localizzata (Woolly Hair Nevus)Non ereditariaChiazza circoscritta su cuoio capelluto sano; talvolta presente in mosaicismo associato a nevi epidermici.
Acquisita (Kinky Hair indotto)Iatrogena / ReattivaRara, secondaria a farmaci (retinoidi sistemici quali acitretina/isotretinoina, inibitori di EGFR) o nelle fasi iniziali di alopecia androgenetica.

SEBORREA E DISFUNZIONE SEBACEA 💧

La seborrea è definita come un'aumentata produzione quantitativa di sebo (seborrea oleosa) o un'alterazione qualitativa della sua composizione lipidica (seborrea sicca). Non è una patologia stante a sé, bensì una disfunzione omeostatica che altera il film idrolipidico di superficie, creando un microambiente idoneo allo sviluppo di acne, forfora e dermatite seborroica.

Classificazione Clinica della Seborrea

Forma ClinicaMeccanismo FisiopatologicoManifestazioni Cutanee & Conseguenze
Seborrea FisiologicaAttività secretoria bilanciata delle ghiandole olocrine regolata da età, sesso, ormoni e genetica.Costituzione della barriera idrolipidica e lubrificazione fisiologica del fusto.
Seborrea Patologica (Oleosa)Iperproduzione quantitativa di sebo.Cute e annessi iper-untuosi, ritenzione sebacea (stasi di sebo ossidato), comedoni e disbiosi (alterazione dell'equilibrio ecologico) del microbiota.
Seborrea SeccaAlterazione qualitativa della frazione lipidica: deficit di acido linoleico ed eccesso di squalene perossidato.Aspetto desquamativo e xerotico (secchezza cutanea patologica), pur in presenza di normo o ipersecrezione ghiandolare.

Fisiopatologia e Meccanismi Molecolari

Cascata Molecolare della Seborrea

Endocrinologia & Microbioma
Stimolo Endocrino
Testosterone → DHT
Sintesi di 5α-diidrotestosterone via 5α-reduttasi di tipo I. Il DHT si lega al recettore androgeno (AR).
Potenziamento Signaling
IGF-1 / Insulina
Attivazione dell'asse mTORC1 che amplifica e co-stimola il pathway lipogenico.
↓
Attivazione Genica
Pathway SREBP-1c
Trascrizione della Sterol Regulatory Element-Binding Protein per la stimolazione diretta della lipogenesi nei sebociti.
Alterazione Lipidica & Perossidazione:
Deplezione di acido linoleico (essenziale per la funzione barriera e la coesione intercheratinocitaria) e aumento relativo di squalene. Lo squalene perossidato (squalene monoidroperossido) induce uno stato pro-infiammatorio e ipercheratosi infundibolare (ispessimento del colletto del follicolo).
Ruolo del Microbiota e Malassezia spp.:
I lieviti lipofili opportunisti Malassezia restricta e M. globosa metabolizzano i trigliceridi sebacei tramite lipasi extracellulari, rilasciando acidi grassi liberi irritanti (es. acido oleico). Penetrazione nello strato corneo con conseguente infiammazione, prurito e desquamazione reattiva.

Conseguenze Cliniche e Diagnosi Differenziale

  • Alopecia Androgenetica: La seborrea agisce da cofattore: la microinfiammazione perifollicolare accelerata dai perossidi lipidici e dal microbiota amplifica la miniaturizzazione dei follicoli suscettibili.
  • Follicolite e Acne Volgare: L'ostruzione del microcomedone crea un ambiente anossico ideale per l'iperproliferazione di Cutibacterium acnes con conseguente cascata infiammatoria.
  • Pitiriasi Steatoide: Condizione intermedia caratterizzata da squame giallastre, unte e aderenti al cuoio capelluto, imbibite di sebo degradato.
  • Dermatite Seborroica: Dermatite cronica recidivante (eritema, desquamazione e prurito) localizzata nelle aree a maggiore densità sebacea, sostenuta dall'interazione tra sebo, Malassezia e risposta immunitaria dell'ospite.

Approccio Terapeutico e Sebo-Regolazione

Il target clinico prevede la riduzione del carico microbico, il ripristino del turnover epidermico e il controllo della lipogenesi, salvaguardando l'integrità della barriera cutanea per prevenire l'effetto rebound (ipersecrezione reattiva compensatoria).

Classe TerapeuticaPrincipi AttiviMeccanismo d'Azione Clinico
Antifungini & AntimicrobiciKetoconazolo / Ciclopirox Olamina
Piroctone Olamina / Zinco Piritione		Ampio spettro contro Malassezia spp.; azione citostatica (blocco della proliferazione cellulare) e normalizzante sul microbiota cutaneo.
Cheratolitici & Sebo-ModulatoriAcido Salicilico / Acido Azelaico
Zinco PCA / Niacinamide		Azione lipofila cheratolitica (rimozione dei tappi cornei), antinfiammatoria, inibizione della 5α-reduttasi e protezione dalla perossidazione dello squalene.
Supporto Fisioterapico & StrumentaleAlta Frequenza
LLLT (Photobiomodulation)		Generazione di ozono ad azione battericida, fungicida e vasomodulante; laser a bassa intensità (LLLT - Low-Level Laser Therapy) per attenuare l'infiammazione e stimolare la riparazione.

FORFORA (PITIRIASIS SIMPLEX CAPITIS) 🌨️

La forfora è una condizione cronica non infiammatoria (o lievemente infiammatoria) caratterizzata da desquamazione visibile del cuoio capelluto. È causata da un accelerato turnover epidermico: il tempo di ricambio dei cheratinociti si riduce da circa 28 giorni a 2–7 giorni. Le cellule non raggiungono la completa maturazione e si aggregano in squame visibili prima di distaccarsi.

Fisiopatologia: Triade Eziologica e Danno di Barriera

Triade Eziopatogenetica della Forfora

Homeostasis Barrier
1. Eccesso di Sebo (Substrato) + 2. Presenza di Malassezia + 3. Suscettibilità Individuale
La patogenesi richiede l'interazione simultanea di tutti e tre i fattori (genetica, assetto immunitario e integrità della barriera).
Ruolo della Malassezia:
La forfora richiede la presenza del lievito lipofilo Malassezia (specie M. globosa e M. restricta). Le sue lipasi idrolizzano i trigliceridi del sebo rilasciando acidi grassi liberi (es. acido oleico). Nei soggetti suscettibili, l'acido oleico penetra nello strato corneo, inducendo irritazione, infiammazione sub-clinica e paracheratosi (persistenza dei nuclei cellulari nello strato corneo dovuta a iperproliferazione).
Alterazione della Barriera Cutanea:
Lo strato corneo forforaico presenta una funzione barriera compromessa e una maggiore permeabilità (TEWL aumentato - Transepidermal Water Loss, o perdita d'acqua transepidermica). Questo favorisce la penetrazione di agenti irritanti e la disidratazione, alimentando un circolo vizioso di secchezza e desquamazione.

Classificazione Clinica della Forfora

VarianteMorfologia delle SquameStato della Cute SottostanteInquadramento Clinico
Pitiriasi Secca (Semplice)Fini, bianche o grigiastre, polverulente e poco aderenti.Normale o lievemente xerotica (secca). Prurito lieve o assente.Tipica della stagione invernale (aria secca).
Pitiriasi Grassa (Steatoide)Grosse, untuose e giallastre, aggregate in placche aderenti.Eritematosa (arrossata), oleosa e infiammata.Forma lieve di dermatite seborroica; richiede un trattamento più aggressivo.

Strategia Terapeutica e Gestione

L'obiettivo terapeutico è controllare la popolazione di Malassezia, normalizzare il turnover cheratinocitario e ridurre l'infiammazione, ripristinando la barriera cutanea.

Categoria FarmacologicaPrincipi AttiviMeccanismo d'Azione Specifico
Agenti Antimicotici• Ketoconazolo (2%)
• Piritione di Zinco (ZPT)
• Ciclopirox Olamina / Solfuro di Selenio		Inibizione della sintesi dell'ergosterolo (componente della membrana fungina); attività fungicida, antibatterica e citostatica per ridurre l'iperproliferazione dei cheratinociti.
Agenti Cheratolitici• Acido Salicilico
• Zolfo		Favoriscono la desquamazione chimica ("scollamento" delle squame) e la penetrazione follicolare; azione sebostatica. Non hanno attività antimicotica diretta.

Correttezza d'Uso e Parametri Chimico-Fisici

Protocollo D'Uso

È fondamentale utilizzare shampoo con un pH acido (4.0–5.5) per rispettare il mantello idrolipidico fisiologico e creare un ambiente sfavorevole alla proliferazione fungina (che preferisce pH neutri o alcalini).

Il tempo di contatto è cruciale: lo shampoo terapeutico deve agire per 3–5 minuti prima del risciacquo. Studi dimostrano che un contatto inferiore a 2 minuti riduce drasticamente l'efficacia antimicotica e citostatica dei principi attivi.

CAPELLI: COME SONO FATTI E IL LORO CICLO VITALE

1. ANATOMIA E STRUTTURA DEL CAPELLO

I peli e i capelli sono filamenti fatti di cheratina. Nascono da un "sacco" nella pelle chiamato FOLLICOLO PILIFERO.

Il follicolo si trova sotto la pelle del cuoio capelluto (derma). La sua parte finale, concava, si chiama BULBO.

La lunghezza, lo spessore e la posizione dei capelli cambiano in base a dove si trovano, al sesso, all'età e alla razza.

Le Parti del Capello

  • La parte che esce dalla pelle si chiama FUSTO (o STELO).
  • La parte sotto la pelle (dentro il follicolo) si chiama RADICE.
  • In fondo alla radice c'è la PAPILLA DERMICA. Questa papilla porta il nutrimento al capello.
  • Tra il bulbo e la radice c'è la MATRICE DEL CAPELLO. La matrice crea tutti i componenti del capello.

Queste parti formano l'APPARATO PILO-SEBACEO.

APPARATO PILO-SEBACEO: COMPONENTI

  • ▶ FOLLICOLO PILIFERO (con il capello)
  • ▶ MUSCOLO PILO ERETTORE
  • ▶ GHIANDOLA SEBACEA

FOLLICOLO PILIFERO:

Il follicolo è un "sacco" della pelle, inclinato, che scende nel derma per 1-3 mm. Contiene il pelo e le sue guaine.

Ogni persona ha circa 5 milioni di follicoli. Circa 100.000 sono sul cuoio capelluto. Questo numero è stabilito prima della nascita e non aumenta più.

GHIANDOLA SEBACEA:

Questa ghiandola produce il sebo, una sostanza grassa (trigliceridi, colesterolo, ecc.).

Il sebo serve a lubrificare, ammorbidire e proteggere il capello man mano che cresce. Il sebo si diffonde sulla pelle e sul capello. La sua attività è controllata da fattori ormonali e alimentari.

MUSCOLO PILO-ERETTORE:

È fatto di fibre muscolari lisce. Si attacca al follicolo.

Quando si contrae (per freddo o emozioni come paura), il pelo si mette dritto. Questo causa la pelle d'oca. Aiuta anche a far uscire il sebo.

2. STRUTTURA DEL CAPELLO

Il capello è una fibra complessa. Contiene acqua (10-30%) e grassi (sebo, cere, ecc.) per proteggersi.

Il fusto del capello ha tre strati:

  • CUTICOLA: È la parte più esterna. È fatta di cellule piatte e sovrapposte, come le tegole di un tetto.
  • CORTECCIA: Si trova sotto la cuticola. È la parte più grande del capello. Dà al capello la sua resistenza e contiene la melanina (colore).
  • MIDOLLO: È la parte centrale, quasi assente nel fusto.

Le molecole principali sono: cheratina (struttura), melanina (colore) e minerali.

CHERATINA: LA STRUTTURA FONDAMENTALE

Il capello è fatto principalmente di cheratina. Ne esistono due tipi:

  • Cheratina Filamentosa: Forma dei fasci (fibrille) nella corteccia.
  • Cheratina Amorfa: Riempie gli spazi tra i fasci, dando stabilità.

COME RIMANE STABILE LA STRUTTURA?

Le catene di cheratina sono unite da dei "ponti" che le tengono insieme. Ci sono 3 tipi di ponti:

1. PONTI IDROGENO

Sono legami molto deboli. Si rompono facilmente con l'acqua o il calore. Danno al capello flessibilità.

2. PONTI SALINI

Sono legami mediamente forti. Si rompono con forte calore o con sostanze acide/basiche. Danno al capello resistenza.

3. PONTI DISOLFURO

Sono legami molto forti (legami covalenti), fatti da atomi di zolfo.

Questi ponti danno struttura (ad esempio i capelli ricci naturali). Possono essere rotti solo con molta energia (es. trattamenti chimici).

I tre tipi di legame contribuiscono tutti alla resistenza del capello.

MINERALI

I minerali sono essenziali. Se mancano, i capelli diventano fragili, secchi e opachi.

I minerali più importanti sono:

  • FERRO: Se manca, causa fragilità e caduta eccessiva.
  • RAME: Fondamentale per il colore (melanina) e per i ponti disolfuro.
  • ZINCO: Indispensabile per la crescita delle cellule.

LIPIDI (GRASSI)

I lipidi provengono per lo più dal sebo.

I fosfolipidi sono importanti perché aiutano a mantenere la corretta idratazione del capello.

MELANINE: IL COLORE NATURALE

La melanina è il pigmento naturale. Si trova nella corteccia ed è prodotta dai melanociti.

I tipi di pigmento sono:

  • EUMELANINA: Colore blu/nero (capelli scuri).
  • FEOMELANINA: Colore giallo/rosso (capelli biondi e rossi).
  • TRICOCROMI: Pigmenti speciali per il colore rosso intenso.

La melanina nasce dall'aminoacido tirosina. La diversa percentuale dei pigmenti determina il colore finale del capello.

3. CICLO VITALE DEL CAPELLO

Il capello ha cicli di crescita e di riposo. Quando un capello vecchio cade, il follicolo ne forma uno nuovo.

Il ciclo ha 3 fasi:

1. ANAGEN: Fase di crescita

È la fase più lunga. La matrice del capello è molto attiva e lo fa crescere.

  • Durata: 2-4 anni nell'uomo, 3-7 anni nella donna.
  • Il capello cresce di circa 1-1,5 cm al mese.

2. CATAGEN: Fase di transizione

È molto breve, dura 2-4 settimane. La matrice smette di lavorare.

3. TELOGEN: Fase di riposo

È il periodo di riposo, dura circa 3 mesi.

Il capello cade solo quando ne sta crescendo uno nuovo che lo spinge fuori.

La caduta dei capelli nell'uomo è a "mosaico": ogni follicolo segue il suo ciclo da solo. Questo assicura che non ci siano periodi senza capelli.

Nota: ogni follicolo può fare fino a 30 cicli di vita.

HAIR: ANATOMY, STRUCTURE, AND LIFE CYCLE

Hair consists of filamentous, keratinized cutaneous appendages (protein structures produced by the skin) originating from the HAIR FOLLICLES: oblique invaginations of the epidermis (slanted channels in the skin) that penetrate the dermis (the deep inner layer), terminating at the base in an expanded, concave structure known as the HAIR BULB. Morphology, topographic distribution, and shaft thickness are determined by genetic, anatomical, hormonal, and ethnic factors.

Anatomically, the pilary unit is divided into three distinct portions: the SHAFT, the visible segment emerging from the skin surface; the ROOT, the intra-follicular portion; and the BULB, the deep basal portion. Within the concavity of the bulb resides the DERMAL PAPILLA, a conical connective tissue structure, richly vascularized and innervated (abundant in blood vessels and nerve endings), essential for nourishment and regulation of the follicular cycle.

The lower portion of the bulb surrounding the papilla constitutes the HAIR MATRIX (germinative layer). This population of undifferentiated cells, exhibiting high mitotic activity (unspecialized cells that divide and multiply rapidly), is responsible for protein synthesis and progressive keratinization (the hardening and maturation process of keratin) that generates all hair components.

The combination of the follicle, the hair, and adjacent glandular and muscular structures constitutes the morpho-functional unit known as the PILO-SEBACEOUS APPARATUS, whose proper function ensures the integrity of the cutaneous barrier and tissue homeostasis (the ideal physiological balance).

The PILO-SEBACEOUS APPARATUS comprises three fundamental structures:

  • The HAIR FOLLICLE, housing the hair root and its associated sheaths.
  • The ARRECTOR PILI (ERECTOR PILI) MUSCLE.
  • The SEBACEOUS GLAND (which, in certain locations, is associated with an apocrine sweat gland).
STRUCTUREDESCRIPTION AND PHYSIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
HAIR FOLLICLEA specialized epidermal structure, obliquely oriented relative to the skin surface, penetrating the dermis to a depth of 1–3 mm. The total number of follicles in humans is genetically determined (approx. 5 million), with about 100,000 localized on the scalp. Follicular morphogenesis (follicle formation during fetal development) is an early process: it begins between the 9th and 12th weeks of gestation and is completed by the 7th month of fetal life; thereafter, no new follicles form de novo (no new follicles are ever formed after birth).
SEBACEOUS GLANDA holocrine exocrine gland (a gland that releases its secretion by completely dissolving its own cells) that secretes sebum into the follicular infundibulum via the sebaceous duct. Sebum, a lipid mixture rich in triglycerides, squalene, waxes, and cholesterol, lubricates, hydrates, and waterproofs the hair cuticle, protecting the skin. Located in the upper portion (infundibulum, i.e., the channel exit) of the follicle, its activity does not interfere with the mitotic processes (cell division) of the hair bulb matrix. Sebum secretion is regulated by endocrine factors (primarily androgen hormones), as well as neural and metabolic stimuli.
ARRECTOR PILI MUSCLEComposed of a bundle of smooth muscle fibers (involuntary muscles), it anchors to the papillary dermis and inserts into the connective tissue sheath of the follicle, just above the sebaceous gland. Its involuntary contraction, mediated by the sympathetic nervous system in response to cold or emotional stimuli (fear, stress), causes the verticalization of the hair shaft (piloerection or "goosebumps"). This mechanical pressure on the underlying sebaceous gland actively facilitates the expulsion of sebum into the follicular lumen (channel).

PILOSEBACEOUS APPARATUS IN DETAIL - THE HAIR: STRUCTURE

The hair shaft is a complex biological structure with a high degree of organization, composed of specific macromolecular and chemical components. Its hydration rate varies from 10% to 30% by weight, closely related to environmental thermohygrometric conditions (air temperature and humidity). The cuticular surface is covered by a lipid film of sebum (composed of triglycerides, waxes, cholesterol, phospholipids, and squalene), which performs an essential barrier function against external chemical-physical insults.

The hair shaft is structured into three concentric layers:

  • Cuticle: the outermost layer, formed by flattened, heavily keratinized cells (up to 6–8 overlapping layers), arranged longitudinally like roof tiles to protect the underlying cortex.
  • Cortex: located beneath the cuticle, it constitutes the predominant component of the shaft. It is formed by fusiform cells (spindle-shaped or elongated) rich in aligned keratin filaments, determining the mechanical properties of resistance and elasticity of the hair. It also houses melanin granules, responsible for pigmentation (natural color).
  • Medulla: the central column of the shaft, often discontinuous or absent in very fine hairs. It consists of loosely connected keratinized cells arranged in rows and interspersed with air-filled vacuoles (micro-spaces containing air) and pigment traces.
en.hair_biochemistry:
In summary: The molecular structure of hair is supported by a complex keratin matrix, stabilized by high- and low-energy chemical bonds that dictate elasticity and shape. The balance between lipids and essential trace elements preserves hydration and mechanical strength, while follicular melanogenesis regulates natural pigmentation and protection against oxidative stress.

HAIR BIOCHEMISTRY

From a biochemical standpoint, the fundamental constituents of hair (excluding water) include keratin (predominantly in hydrophobic α-conformation, a protein structure that repels water with high resistance), structural and surface lipids, melanin pigments (eumelanin and pheomelanin), and a fraction of essential trace elements and minerals in atomic state (such as iron, zinc, magnesium, and calcium).

KERATIN AND ULTRASTRUCTURE

Hair keratins are classified into two structural types: filamentous keratin and amorphous protein matrix. Filamentous keratin forms a complex ultrastructure organized into bundles or fibrils within the cortex, while the amorphous protein matrix fills the spaces between fibrils, stabilizing their architecture. The polypeptide chains (linked amino acid chains) coil around themselves into a DNA-like helical shape.

Keratin macromolecules, composed of long polypeptide chains, are laterally stabilized and held together by interchain chemical bonds (cross-links) formed between amino acid residues of adjacent filaments.

Types of keratin chemical bonds and their impact on physiological resistance
Bond TypeNature and SensitivityPhysiological Role and Properties
Hydrogen BondsREF #9(see reference 9 on keratin genetics in the bibliography at the bottom of the page)
Weak electrostatic interactions, easily cleaved by water and heat (the basis of temporary thermal styling).Established between the carbonyl oxygen (-C=O) and amide hydrogen (-NH-) of the peptide backbone. Intrachain bonds stabilize the α-helix, while interchain bonds provide flexibility and reversible elasticity.
Salt Bridges (Ionic Interactions)REF #9(see reference 9 on keratin genetics in the bibliography at the bottom of the page)
Medium-energy bonds, sensitive to extreme temperature shifts and sharp pH changes (acidic or basic solutions).Electrostatic interactions between ionized side chains of acidic (glutamic acid, aspartic acid) and basic (lysine, arginine) amino acids. Highly abundant, they are critical for tensile strength.
Disulfide BondsREF #9(see reference 9 on keratin genetics in the bibliography at the bottom of the page)
Strong covalent bonds (irreversible by water/heat alone), formed by the oxidation of thiol groups (-SH) in cysteine to form cystine (-S-S-).Primary stabilizing factor for tertiary and quaternary structures. They dictate rigidity, permanent shape (curl pattern), and chemical-physical resistance. Require redox chemical treatments (perming, chemical straightening).

Although hydrogen and salt bonds possess lower individual binding energy, their exceptionally high numerical density means each of the three bond classes contributes approximately 1/3 to the overall mechanical strength and shape stability of the hair.

The spatial configuration, density, and geometric regularity of these bonds (particularly disulfide bond architecture) determine the macromolecular organization of the cortex and, consequently, the morphological hair phenotype (straight, wavy, curly).

TRACE ELEMENTS AND MINERALS

Minerals constitute essential biochemical and catalytic components for hair homeostasis (metabolic balance). Mineral deficiencies impair keratogenesis (keratin synthesis), leading to brittleness, dryness, loss of luster, and follicular cycle abnormalities (telogen effluvium or excessive shedding).

Quantitative distribution and clinical-biochemical role of key minerals in the hair shaft
Trace ElementConcentrationBiochemical and Clinical Function
Iron4 - 12 μg/gEssential enzymatic cofactor; deficiency (sideropenia) impairs bulb matrix proliferation leading to weakening. Highly concentrated in red hair (pheomelanin).
Magnesium30 - 45 μg/gActivator in enzymatic complexes and ATP synthesis (cellular energy molecule), vital for protein biosynthesis. Abundant in dark hair.
Copper16 - 50 μg/gCatalytic core of the tyrosinase enzyme, essential for melanogenesis (pigment production). Participates in catalyzing disulfide bond formation.
Zinc150 - 180 μg/gFundamental trace element for polymerase activity and cell division in the bulb. Chronic deficiency inhibits cell turnover causing shaft fragility and dystrophy.

The endogenous mineral component regulates intrinsic hair fiber hydration through hygroscopic balance (moisture-retention capacity); loss of bound water alters macrofibril alignment, compromising structural cohesion.

STRUCTURAL AND SURFACE LIPIDS

REF #3(see reference 3 by Wertz & Downing on hair lipids in the bibliography at the bottom of the page)

Lipids are divided into exogenous (sebaceous origin: triglycerides, waxes, squalene, free fatty acids coating the cuticle) and endogenous (structural lipids integrated into the cell membrane and CMC - Cell Membrane Complex, such as cholesterol and cholesterol sulfate).

Of fundamental structural significance are phospholipids and ceramides, intrinsic constituents of cell membranes. Due to their amphipathic nature (ability to bind both water and fats), they modulate hydrophobicity and permeability, regulating water fluxes and ensuring hydration, elasticity, and intercellular cohesion between cuticular and cortical cells.

MELANINS AND CHROMATIC PHENOTYPE

REF #4(see reference 4 by Valverde et al. on MC1R gene and pheomelanin in the bibliography at the bottom of the page)

Melanin is the natural pigmented polymer localized predominantly in the cortex. It is synthesized within melanosomes (specialized organelles) by melanocytes in the hair bulb. The concentration and ratio between these polymers dictate the natural color spectrum (canities or graying results from the cessation of melanogenesis).

Dark Pigment
Eumelanin
→ Brown and black tones
High molecular weight insoluble polymer localized in large ellipsoidal melanosomes. Absorbs the light spectrum, protecting the fiber from photodamage.
Light Pigment
Pheomelanin
→ Blonde and red tones
Sulfur-containing polymer with spherical, dispersed melanosomes. Reflects yellow/orange tones, imparting warm shades across the chromatic scale.
Rutilous VariantREF #4(see reference 4 on MC1R gene)
Rutilous Phenotype and MC1R Genetics
→ Natural red hair and genetic regulation
Natural red hair results from a predominance of pheomelanin (red-yellow-sulfur pigment) relative to eumelanin. The phenotype is determined by recessive loss-of-function genetic variants in the MC1R gene (chromosome 16), which impair receptor activity and block eumelanin synthesis, favoring the pheomelanin pathway.

RESEARCH INSIGHT | Melanin Biosynthesis (Melanogenesis)

REF #4 DOI(opens the hair color genetics study by Valverde et al. in Nature Genetics in a new tab)

The universal precursor of the pathway is the amino acid L-tyrosine. In eumelanin synthesis, tyrosine is hydroxylated into L-DOPA and oxidized into dopaquinone via tyrosinase (a copper-dependent metalloprotein enzyme). Through sequential stages of cyclization and oxidative polymerization, dopaquinone evolves into insoluble macromolecules. Catalytic efficiency determines final pigment intensity.

Pheomelanin synthesis occurs in the presence of a critical concentration of cysteine (or glutathione): cysteine binds to dopaquinone forming cysteinyldopa, which generates yellow-orange pigments through subsequent oxidations.

Oculocutaneous albinism represents the primary pathological model of this pathway: mutations in the tyrosinase gene alter the enzyme's tertiary structure, inhibiting tyrosine conversion and resulting in total absence of pigment synthesis.

The reciprocal percentage variation and volumetric density of these fractions genetically define the entire spectrum of natural hair tones and shades.
en.life_cycle_section:
THE HAIR FOLLICLE LIFE CYCLE

The hair follicle is a dynamic organ characterized by asynchronous cyclic activity (where each hair follows its own independent rhythm), alternating between growth, regression, and resting phases. Under physiological conditions, the shedding of a telogen hair coincides with the initiation of a new anagen cycle within the same follicle. Polytrichia phenomena (the presence of multiple hair shafts emerging from a single ostium or pore) occur predominantly in scalp follicular units, where distinct follicles share a sebaceous gland and a common pilary canal.

The biological hair cycle is classically divided into three main phases: anagen, catagen, and telogen.

- Growth phase (ANAGEN):

Anagen consists of 6 sub-phases (anagen I to VI). The biological process begins with the activation of stem cells in the bulge niche (the follicular swelling zone acting as a regenerative reservoir) and matrix, triggering intense mitotic activity (cell replication) until the complete formation of the new hair shaft. On the scalp, anagen has an average duration of 2–4 years in men and 3–7 years in women. Consequently, loss of mature hair is compensated by the genesis of a new terminal strand. In other body regions, anagen is drastically shorter: 1–6 months for eyelashes and 20–40 days for limb vellus hair.

Anagen duration is genetically determined and regulates maximum hair length. The kinetic growth rate is approximately 1–1.5 cm per month, with faster rates generally observed in females. This phase varies by ethnicity (reaching its maximum in straight, circular-section Asian hair) and scalp topography: occipital follicles exhibit longer anagen phases than temporal ones, while vertical proliferation speed is statistically higher at the vertex compared to the occiput.

In follicles affected by androgenetic alopecia (common pattern baldness), a progressive shortening of the anagen phase occurs (down to 3–5 months), associated with follicular miniaturization, which limits shaft length to a few centimeters and transforms its structure into vellus hair (fine, unpigmented, medullaless hair). Biological aging (chronological aging) also physiologically reduces anagen duration and shaft diameter.

Scientific Note

REF #2(see reference 2 by Cotsarelis et al. in the bibliography at the bottom of the page)

The replicative potential of the follicle is not mathematically predetermined locally, but is bound to the stem cell pool and organism longevity. Over an average human lifespan, an individual follicle completes approximately 25–30 cycles prior to senescence.

Cycle PhaseBiological StateAverage Duration (Scalp)Key Characteristic
ANAGENActive Growth2–4 years (Men) / 3–7 years (Women)Intense mitotic activity and keratin synthesis.
CATAGENInvolution / Apoptosis2–4 weeksPigmentation arrest and dermal papilla upward migration.
TELOGENMetabolic RestingApprox. 3 monthsFormation of the "club hair" bulb prior to shedding.
EXOGENActive DetachmentFinal stage of TelogenEnzymatic process of shaft ejection from the follicle.
KENOGENLatency / Empty FollicleVariable (physiological or pathological)Time interval between shedding and a new anagen cycle.

- Involution and apoptosis phase (CATAGEN):

This is a transient involutive phase lasting 2–4 weeks. During catagen, matrix keratinocytes undergo programmed apoptosis (controlled cell self-destruction), melanin synthesis ceases, and the lower portion of the follicle regresses, causing the dermal papilla to migrate upward toward the upper dermal layers (bulge region).

- Functional resting and shedding phase (TELOGEN and EXOGEN):

Telogen represents the metabolic quiescence period (functional rest) of the follicle, lasting an average of about 3 months. Mitotic activity is absent and the anchoring sheaths keratinize, giving the hair base its classic "club-shaped" structure. The actual detachment of the shaft from the follicle (now independently classified as the exogen phase) is an active process regulated by proteolytic enzymes that degrade the hair-follicle junction, often facilitated by the mechanical push of the new anagen hair, ensuring continuous hair turnover.

If the follicle remains empty for a latent period between the shedding of the old hair and the start of a new anagen, this is defined as the kenogen phase. Although this empty interval accounts for a minimal percentage in a healthy scalp, it undergoes a significant and pathological increase in androgenetic alopecia.

Traumatic or mechanical extraction of a telogen hair triggers a biochemical signal that interrupts follicular quiescence, stimulating the early onset of a new anagen cycle. The characteristic whitish bulb visible at the base of spontaneously shed hair is not a "live root", but rather the keratinized, unpigmented bulb typical of the telogen phase.

Unlike many mammals that undergo synchronous molting, human hair replacement follows an asynchronous "mosaic pattern": each follicle evolves independently from adjacent ones. However, systemic fluctuations and photoperiod variations (hours of sunlight) can induce partial follicle synchronization, clinically evident as physiological seasonal shedding during transitional seasons (autumn and spring).

From a strictly cyto-functional perspective (regarding cell behavior and function), follicular activity is divided into two macro-phases:

  • A proliferative and morphogenetic phase: characterized by the rapid downward extension of the keratinocyte column invading the deep dermis, corresponding to the early sub-phases of anagen (anagen I to V);
  • A differentiative and synthetic phase: predominant during anagen VI, where mitotic activity stabilizes at the baseline level necessary to sustain continuous keratinization and protein synthesis of the shaft. Subsequent catagen represents mitotic arrest with terminal differentiation of residual cells, while telogen constitutes the biosynthetic silence required for structural reorganization of the follicular unit.

The temporal heterogeneity of the hair cycle across different anatomical regions (e.g., an inverted anagen/telogen ratio in eyebrows and pubic hair compared to the scalp) accounts for the varying biological length of body hair and explains the selective susceptibility of follicles to specific dermatoses, autoimmune, or hormone-dependent conditions.

THE ATOM AND CHEMICAL BONDS ⚛️

The atom is the smallest particle of a chemical element that retains its specific characteristics and identity.

Main Components

It consists of:

Center of Mass
Nucleus
→ Protons and Neutrons
Composed of protons (positive charge) and neutrons (uncharged). It concentrates almost all the atom's mass (>99.9%).
Electron Cloud
Electrons
→ Quantum Mechanical Model
Negatively charged particles moving around the nucleus occupying orbitals, regions of space where there is a maximum probability of finding them.

Fundamental Concept

Neutral State
Charge Balance
An electrically neutral atom has an equal number of protons and electrons, resulting in a net charge = 0.

Ions 🧪

An ION is an atom (or group of atoms) that has lost or gained one or more electrons, acquiring a net electrical charge.

Electron Gain
Anion
→ Negative Charge (-)
Formed by gaining electrons by the atom; the resulting electrical charge is net and negative.
Electron Loss
Cation
→ Positive Charge (+)
Formed by losing electrons by the atom; the resulting electrical charge is net and positive.

Periodic Table of Elements 📊

Elements are arranged by increasing atomic number (Z), according to the principle of periodicity formulated by Mendeleev in 1869.

Cell Content

Periodic Table
Typical Cell Structure
  1. In the center: the chemical symbol (e.g., Na, Cl).
  2. Highlighted: the atomic number Z (number of protons; defines the identity of the element).
  3. At the bottom: the relative atomic mass (expressed in u, unified atomic mass units; it is the weighted average of its natural isotope masses).

Chemical Bonds and Stability 🔗

Atoms interact to reach a state of minimum potential energy, forming more stable aggregates.

Guiding Principle
Bond Spontaneity
The bond forms spontaneously because the resulting system has a lower energy content compared to isolated atoms. Lower potential energy = greater stability.

Lewis and Valence Theory

Atoms interact to achieve a stable outer electron configuration (minimum energy), often similar to that of noble gases.

The Octet Rule

Noble gases (Group 18) are chemically inert because they have a complete valence shell: 8 electrons (octet), except helium which is stable with 2 (duet).

Rule: “Atoms tend to lose, gain, or share electrons to achieve the electron configuration of the nearest noble gas (8 outer electrons, or 2 for H and He).”

Scientific note: This rule is an excellent approximation for period 2 and 3 elements, but exceptions exist (e.g., electron-deficient molecules, expanded octets in higher periods).

Bond Energy ⚡

Thermodynamic Parameter
Bond Energy and Distance
Bond energy is the minimum energy required to break one mole of chemical bonds in the gaseous state (kJ/mol). High values indicate strong bonds and thermodynamically stable molecules. The bond distance is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of the bonded atoms.

STRONG BONDS (INTRAMOLECULAR) 🔩

1. Ionic Bond

Δχ ≥ 1.7
Electrostatic Attraction
→ Almost complete electron transfer

Electrostatic attraction force established between oppositely charged ions. It typically forms between a metal and a non-metal with a high electronegativity difference.

Formation Mechanism:
  1. Transfer of valence electrons between atoms.
  2. The less electronegative atom loses electrons (becomes a cation).
  3. The more electronegative atom gains electrons (becomes an anion).

It does not form isolated molecules, but ordered three-dimensional structures called crystal lattices (e.g., NaCl).

2. Covalent Bond

Formed by electron sharing between non-metallic atoms with similar or identical electronegativity (Δχ < 1.7).

Types of Covalent Bond:
Δχ ≤ 0.4
Nonpolar Covalent (Homopolar)
→ e.g., H₂, O₂, CH₄
Established between identical atoms or atoms with negligible electronegativity difference. The electron cloud is symmetrically distributed between the two nuclei.
0.4 < Δχ < 1.7
Polar Covalent
→ e.g., HCl, H₂O
Electrons are drawn closer to the more electronegative atom, generating a partial negative charge (δ⁻) on it and a positive one (δ⁺) on the other, forming an electric dipole.
Coordination
Dative Covalent Bond
→ e.g., H₃O⁺, NH₄⁺ (Symbol: →)
The shared electron pair originates entirely from a single atom (donor, possessing a lone pair) and is accepted into an empty orbital of the other atom (acceptor). Once formed, it is indistinguishable from a standard covalent bond.

*Note: Exceptions to the octet rule exist, such as incomplete octets (e.g., boron compounds), expanded octets (e.g., SF6), or odd-electron molecules.

3. Metallic Bond ⚙️

Drude-Lorentz Model
Sea of Electrons
Consists of a geometric lattice of positive ions immersed in a diffuse cloud of highly delocalized valence electrons free to move throughout the solid. Cohesion is ensured by omnidirectional electrostatic attraction between mobile electrons and ionic cores.

WEAK BONDS (Intermolecular Forces) 💧

Weak bonds possess a bond energy significantly lower than interatomic (intramolecular) bonds, but are essential in determining the macroscopic properties and physical state of molecular compounds.

Van der Waals Interactions
Dipole-Dipole & Dispersion
Include dipole-dipole interactions (between polar molecules) and London dispersion forces (present in all molecules, but dominant in nonpolar ones).
20–25 kJ/mol
Hydrogen Bond
Very strong dipole-dipole interaction. Established when a hydrogen atom is bonded to small, highly electronegative atoms (F, O, N) and is attracted to nearby lone electron pairs.
Anomalous Behavior
Hydrogen Bonding in Water

In Ice: Forces molecules into a tetrahedral geometry (open hexagonal lattice), increasing volume and decreasing density, allowing ice to float.

In Liquid Phase: Bonds continuously break and reform, conferring high cohesion, high surface tension, and high phase transition points.

CHEMICAL REACTIONS, INORGANIC COMPOUNDS AND MIXTURES 🧪⚗️

In summary: Chemical reactions and the classification of inorganic compounds describe the transformations and properties of matter based on molecular bonds and acid-base behavior. The study of dispersed and colloidal systems integrates formulation chemistry, distinguishing between homogeneous solutions and stable heterogeneous mixtures.

CHEMICAL REACTIONS: TYPES AND REPRESENTATION

A chemical reaction is a process in which chemical bonds are broken and/or formed, resulting in the redistribution of atoms and the transformation of reactants into products with different chemical properties.

Chemical Equation

A chemical equation is the qualitative and quantitative representation of a reaction, where reactants are written on the left and products on the right:

REACTANTS → PRODUCTS

Classification of Reactions (by Mechanism)

Scheme: A + B → AB
1. Synthesis
Two or more substances (elements or compounds) combine to form a single, more complex compound.
Scheme: AB → A + B
2. Decomposition
A compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances through energy input (thermolysis, electrolysis, or photolysis).
Scheme: A + BC → AC + B
3. Single Displacement
A free, more reactive element replaces and displaces another less reactive element present in a compound.
Scheme: AB + CD → AD + CB
4. Double Displacement
Two compounds in solution exchange their constituents (ions) to form new compounds (often with the formation of a precipitate, gas, or water).

Thermodynamics and Reversibility

Symbol: ⇌
Reversible Reactions
Dynamic equilibrium
Products react with each other to reform reactants, reaching a state where the forward reaction rate equals the reverse reaction rate.
Symbol: →
Irreversible Reactions
Unidirectional completion
Proceed almost completely toward product formation until the limiting reactant is exhausted. Stable products do not spontaneously restore reactants.

INORGANIC COMPOUNDS 🔬

Chemical substances typically characterized by the absence of carbon-hydrogen (C-H) bonds. Unlike organic compounds, most do not contain carbon; however, certain carbon-containing species (such as carbon oxides, carbonates, bicarbonates, carbides, and cyanides) are classified as inorganic due to their chemical properties and behavior analogous to mineral salts.

Examples: CO2 (Carbon dioxide), SO3 (Sulfur trioxide).

MIXTURES AND DISPERSED SYSTEMS

A mixture is a physico-chemical system consisting of two or more pure substances coexisting without reacting. Dispersed systems, defined by a dispersing phase (continuous) and a dispersed phase, are classified based on the degree of dispersion and thermodynamic homogeneity:

Polyphasic
Suspensions and Emulsions
→ Heterogeneous Systems (> 1 µm)
Thermodynamically or kinetically unstable systems. Suspensions (solid in liquid) and emulsions (immiscible liquids O/W and W/O) maintain defined interfaces between phases.
Micro-Heterogeneous
Colloidal Systems
→ Colloidal Dispersions (1 - 1000 nm)
Exhibit high surface area and prolonged kinetic stability. They manifest optical properties such as the Tyndall effect and are divided into lyophilic and lyophobic.
Monophasic
True Solutions
→ Molecular Dispersion (< 1 nm)
Thermodynamically stable homogeneous systems where the solute is fully dissolved in the solvent until reaching the solubility limit and saturation equilibrium.

RESEARCH INSIGHT | Association Colloids and Formulation Example

Association colloids arise from the spontaneous self-assembly of amphiphilic molecules (surfactants) possessing a hydrophilic polar head and a hydrophobic non-polar tail. Upon reaching the Critical Micelle Concentration (CMC), these molecules organize into micelles, reducing the system's free energy.

In colloidal phase transitions, a distinction is made between GELS (high-viscosity biphasic systems with a continuous 3D network) and SOLS (fluid colloidal suspensions).

Formulation Example (O/W Moisturizing Cream): The structured emulsifying network (Polyglyceryl-4-Stearate, Cetearyl Glucoside) stabilizes the O/W interface. Amphiphilic consistency agents like Cetyl Alcohol and lipidic factors such as Cera Alba modify the rheology and final texture of the formulation.

The physico-chemical behavior of mixtures and the rheological response of colloidal systems form the application basis for developing stable cosmetic-pharmaceutical preparations and formulations.

pH: DEFINITION, THERMODYNAMICS, AND BIOLOGICAL IMPORTANCE 🧬

In summary: pH measures the thermodynamic activity of hydronium ions in solution. Maintaining pH within tight physiological limits is fundamental for protein stability, metabolic reactions, cellular function, and skin homeostasis.

The pH (potential of hydrogen) is a logarithmic scale (where each 1-unit shift represents a 10-fold change in acidity) quantifying the acidity or alkalinity of an aqueous solution. Thermodynamically, it is defined as the negative base-10 logarithm of the activity of hydronium ions (H3O+):

pH = -log10(aH3O+) = -log10(γ · [H3O+])

Where γ is the activity coefficient (a correction factor for inter-particle interactions; in dilute solutions ≈ 1). In highly dilute solutions (γ → 1), activity approximates molar concentration: pH ≈ -log10[H3O+]. It reflects the dynamic equilibrium governed by the ion product of water (Kw).

SCALE AND CLASSIFICATION

pH < 7
Acidic Environment
[H3O+] > [OH−]
Species capable of donating protons (H+). Strength depends on the acid dissociation constant (Ka) where pKa = -log10(Ka).
  • Strong Acids (pKa < 0): Complete dissociation in water (e.g., HCl, HNO3).
  • Weak Acids (pKa > 0): Partial equilibrium; protonated and ionized forms coexist depending on pH (e.g., Citric Acid, AHAs).
pH = 7
Neutrality Point
Pure water at 25°C
The activity of H3O+ exactly equals that of OH− ions ([H3O+] = [OH−] = 10-7 M).
  • Ion Product: Kw = [H3O+][OH−] = 10-14 at 25°C.
  • Thermal Dependence: At body temperature (37°C), Kw increases and neutrality shifts to pH ~6.81.
pH > 7
Alkaline / Basic Environment
[H3O+] < [OH−]
Species capable of accepting protons (H+) or releasing hydroxide ions (OH−), governed by pKb.
  • Strong Bases: Complete dissociation with direct release of OH− (e.g., NaOH, KOH).
  • Weak Bases: Partial deprotonation of the solvent to establish basic equilibrium (e.g., Triethanolamine, Ammonia).

BIOLOGICAL RELEVANCE AND HOMEOSTASIS

The human organism, composed of 60–70% water, requires strict regulation of ionic concentrations. Physiological blood pH of around 7.4 (range 7.35–7.45) is essential to preserve the electric charge, native conformation, and functionality of structural and enzymatic proteins.

At the subcellular level, pH compartmentalization governs metabolic pathways: the endo-lysosomal system requires progressive acidification down to pH 4.5–5.0 to activate acidic hydrolases responsible for degrading cellular debris.

SKIN pH, EUDERMIA AND BIOLOGICAL DEFENSE 🛡️

The application of topical formulations interacts directly with the stratum corneum and hydrolipidic film. Maintaining eudermia means respecting the physiological acidic gradient to protect barrier function and prevent irritation.

Epidermal Acid Mantle
Body Skin
pH 4.5 – 6.0 (Average: 5.5)
Acidic matrix composed of sebum, sweat (Lactic Acid), and NMF (Natural Moisturizing Factor) components.
  • Lipid Synthesis: Activates β-glucocerebrosidase for ceramide production.
  • Desmosomal Lysis: Regulates serine proteases (KLK5/KLK7) for physiological desquamation.
Adnexal Acid Mantle
Scalp
pH 4.2 – 5.0
Follicular microenvironment with high glandular density.
  • Cuticle Integrity: Prevents swelling of the hair shaft keratin.
  • Microbiome Control: Inhibits hyper-proliferation of Malassezia spp. (a yeast naturally present on the scalp, often linked to dandruff).

CONSEQUENCES OF SKIN pH ALTERATIONS

Neutral-Alkaline Shift (pH ≥ 6.0)
Virulence Switch & Dysbiosis
Altered surface charges and inactivation of lipid synthesis enzymes.
  • Acne Pathogenesis: Upregulation of lipases in Cutibacterium acnes.
  • Pathogenic Colonization: Proliferation of Staphylococcus aureus and loss of corneal cohesion.
Excessive Acidification (pH < 4.5)
Irritation & Barrier Damage
Exceeding the physiological skin buffering capacity.
  • Symptomatology: Triggers erythema, neuropathic burning, and pruritus.
  • Structural Damage: Superficial protein denaturation and suppression of commensal flora.

OPTIMAL pH BY CATEGORY AND FORMULATION REGULATION 🧪

Eudermic and functional pH ranges for cosmetic product types
Product Category Target pH Formulation & Physiological Rationale
Face / Body Cream 5.5 – 6.0 Eudermic, isolipidico (respects and replenishes natural skin lipids) with the hydrolipidic film.
Cleansing Milk 6.0 – 7.0 Affinity cleansing and effective makeup removal.
Facial Toner 4.5 – 5.5 Rapid post-cleansing restoration of the acid mantle.
Technical Exfoliant (High Conc.) ~3.5 Promotes desmosome dissolution (AHA/BHA).
Sensitive Skin Exfoliant ~4.5 Moderate keratolytic action with reduced penetration depth.
Eye Contour 6.5 – 7.2 Iso-lacrimal: aligned with tear film pH (~7.4) to prevent reflex tearing.
Intimate Wash 4.0 – 4.5 High protective acidity for mucosal tissue and Döderlein flora.
Shampoo / Hair Conditioner 4.5 – 5.0 Promotes cuticle closure and keratin fiber compactness.
Traditional Anhydrous Soap 9.5 – 10.5 Chemical requirement of saponification reaction (net alkalinity).

RESEARCH INSIGHT | Analytical Regulation & Stock Solutions % w/w

To adjust pH in laboratory settings, operate under constant stirring by adding adjusting solutions dropwise. To guarantee analytical reproducibility regardless of thermal fluctuations, reagents must be prepared strictly on a weight/weight (% w/w) basis totaling 100 g:

  • Citric Acid 20% (w/w): 20 g Citric Acid + 80 g Purified Water (Hydrophilic acidifier).
  • Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH) 10-18% (w/w): 10–18 g NaOH + Purified Water q.s. to 100 g (Corrosive: handle with PPE).
  • Sodium Bicarbonate 5-10% (w/w): Weak buffer solution for controlled adjustments up to pH ~8.3.

pH & HAIR: ELECTROSTATICS, CUTICLE AND INCI REGULATIONS 💇

ISOELECTRIC POINT AND SURFACE CHARGE

Hair shaft integrity is governed by the net electrical charge of keratin. Hair exhibits a deep isoelectric point (pI) (the pH at which net electrical charge is zero, reducing reactivity) between 3.67 and 4.5, and a surface iso-charge point at pH ~5.0.

Physiological pH (4.5 – 5.5)
Closed Cuticle & Shine
Minimal net surface charge state on the hair shaft.
  • Scale Adhesion: Maintains a compact, sealed structure protecting the cortex.
  • Optico-Mechanical Properties: Reduces inter-fiber friction and maximizes light reflection.
Alkaline pH (> 7.0)
Electrostatic Repulsion & Swelling
Deprotonation of carboxylic (-COOH) and thiol groups in keratin.
  • Negative Charge Generation: Repulsion between cuticle scales forces them open.
  • Structural Damage: Water swelling, frizz effect, and high susceptibility to breakage.

INCI REGULATIONS & RAW MATERIAL CLASSIFICATION

Under Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, ingredient labeling declarations follow strict quantitative rules:

Hierarchy for ingredient listing in INCI labeling
Quantitative Threshold INCI Nomenclature Rule
Concentration > 1% w/w Listed in descending order of weight at the time of batch incorporation.
Concentration < 1% w/w May be listed in arbitrary order, following ingredients present at >1%.
Cosmetic Colorants Identified by Colour Index code (e.g., CI 42090) and listed in any order at the end of the INCI.

FUNCTIONAL CLASSES OF INGREDIENTS

• Surfactants: Anionic, cationic, amphoteric, and non-ionic for cleansing and wetting.
• Emulsifiers: Lipophilic/hydrophilic agents for O/W or W/O interface stabilization.
• Rheology Modifiers: Hydrocolloid polymers and gums for viscosity and yield stress control.
• Humectants: Hygroscopic polyols (Glycerin, Glycols) for free water retention.
• Lipids & Emollients: Oils, butters, esters, and silicones for lipid replenishment.
• Chelating Agents: Complexing agents (EDTA, Phytic Acid) to neutralize metal cations and prevent oxidation.

Hair Formulations: Chemistry and Functionality 💇‍♀️

Cosmetic ingredients can originate from mineral, animal, vegetable, or synthetic sources (lab-created through controlled chemical reactions), which currently make up the majority of components to ensure stability and reproducibility.

US Approach

American Philosophy

Historically focused on stability, sensory appeal, and performance, favoring high-performance synthetic or mineral ingredients.
EU Reg. 1223/2009

European Philosophy

Adopts the precautionary principle (a precautionary approach limiting substances before they cause harm), with strict regulations on toxicological safety, sustainability, and biodegradability.

Role of Denatured Alcohol

Denatured alcohol (ethanol rendered unsuitable for food use via denatonium benzoate) is a ubiquitous component (omnipresent in formulas) with three main technical functions:

Solvent

Solvent Action

Dissolves resins, fats, and water-insoluble organic substances.
Delivery

Excipient & Carrier

Facilates active ingredient penetration into the shaft and delivers a quick cooling sensation via evaporation.
Hygiene & Viscosity

Antiseptic & Co-solvent

Reduces microbial load and lowers viscosity in gel formulations, improving fluid dynamics.

Sprays, Hairsprays, and Propellants

Modern aerosol propellants are light hydrocarbons (Butane, Isobutane, Propane), replacing CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons, old gases damaging to the atmosphere) banned under the Montreal Protocol. Modern propellants feature an ODP (Ozone Depletion Potential) = 0, although classified as VOCs (Volatile Organic Compounds) with a potential global warming impact.

In hairsprays, alongside alcohols, volatile solvents (e.g., ethers or acetates) are utilized to promote rapid evaporation and film formation. Chlorinated solvents (e.g., dichloromethane) have been virtually phased out due to high toxicity.

Functional Additives, Preservatives, and Strengthening Agents

Bio-Tech Insight
  • Vitamins (Niacinamide - Vit. B₃): Precursor to NAD/NADP coenzymes, essential for cellular energy metabolism and ceramide synthesis (the lipid "building blocks" of hair), boosting barrier strength and shine.
  • Panthenol (Provitamin B₅): Converts to pantothenic acid on the scalp (constituent of Coenzyme A); serves as a powerful hygroscopic humectant on the hair shaft, elevating hydration, elasticity, and tensile strength.
  • Preservatives & Boosters: Permitted long-chain parabens used within legal limits (e.g., Butylparaben max 0.14% under EU Reg.). Propylene Glycol acts as a humectant and preservative booster by depressing water activity (aw) available for bacteria.

Gels, Mousse, and Holding Power

Gels are water-/alcohol-based fixatives with high polymer content, whereas Mousses offer a lighter hold courtesy of their aerated structure.

  • Fatty Excipients: Plant-derived additions (e.g., castor oil) to impart film flexibility and reduce flaking or stiffness.
  • Thickeners (Gums): Cellulose derivatives (Hydroxyethylcellulose, Hydroxypropylcellulose) increase aqueous phase viscosity, stabilize foam, and enhance hold performance.

Film-Forming Agents and Natural Feel

Film Formers are polymers (molecular chains) that form a continuous coating over the hair shaft, adding body, texture, and slip. Formulations have evolved from rigid polymers to advanced hybrid systems.

Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP): A classic hydrophilic (water-loving) polymer. It forms a rigid, crystal-clear, water-soluble film responsible for the traditional wet look and crispness in high humidity.

Modern Systems (PVP + Silicone): Adding Polydimethylsiloxane (silicone) forms a hydrophobic outer shield that guards PVP from atmospheric moisture. Maintains structural hold without a wet look, ensuring a natural finish and ease of combing.

In styling mousses, a silicone copolymer (e.g., Dimethicone Copolyol) is routinely used to stabilize foam and aid distribution. The hydrophilic polyether block imparts water/alcohol solubility, while the silicone segment delivers shine and reduces stickiness.

Warnings for Fixatives and Trichorrhexis

Overusing gels or hairsprays, particularly on fragile or chemically treated hair, can stiffen the shaft, rendering it susceptible to mechanical fracture. Aggressive dry removal (dry brushing) of polymer build-up can induce Trichorrhexis Nodosa (shaft breakage featuring a "paintbrush" appearance). Fixatives should always be removed using a gentle lukewarm water wash, never by force through dry brushing.

Hair Dyes: Chemical Classification

Hair coloring relies on the selective absorption of light by chromophore molecules. Dyes are categorized based on their working mechanism and permanence:

Chemical classification of hair dyes by mechanism of action and durability
Dye TypeMechanism of ActionPermanence & Notes
Plant-Based (Henna)Deposits on outer cuticle/cortex through non-covalent interactions (weak bonds like hydrogen and Van der Waals).Lacks stable covalent bonds.
TemporaryHigh-molecular-weight molecules (large molecules unable to enter the hair shaft) adhering strictly to the surface.Washes out with 1st shampoo.
Direct (Semi-Permanent)Small molecules with slight cortical penetration without oxidation (no chemical reaction with peroxide).Lasts: 6-8 washes.
Demi-PermanentLow-development oxidative system (low hydrogen peroxide), penetrates without lightening natural base.Lasts: 20-25 washes.
Permanent (Oxidative)Colorless precursors + H2O2 (hydrogen peroxide) + alkalizing agent (e.g., ammonia) create insoluble pigments.Permanent, stable structural modification.

HAIR COLORATION MECHANISMS 🎨

1. Henna (Natural Substantive Coloration)

Unlike oxidative dyes, henna uses no harsh alkalizing agents. Its active pigment, lawsone (2-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone), diffuses through the cuticle and binds stably to keratin via covalent bonds formed through a Michael addition reaction with the hair's thiol and amino groups. Bond formation is optimized by warm temperatures and a mildly acidic environment.

  • Coloring Agent: Lawsone, extracted from Lawsonia inermis leaves.
  • Structural Impact: Forms a translucent protective shield that increases shaft diameter, tensile strength, and shine, sealing cuticles without damaging internal protein structures.

Beyond coloring, lawsone exhibits potent sebum-regulating, antifungal, and antibacterial properties. Hair gains body and hydration, with enhanced curl definition and superior barrier protection against heat and environmental stress.

Pure Henna

100% Lawsonia Inermis

Does not prevent dark or tone-on-tone chemical dyes. However, the lawsone coating impairs new pigment absorption and makes bleaching or lightening nearly impossible, inevitably yielding bright copper tones.
Metallic Salts

Incompatibility & Risk

Warning: If the blend contains added sodium picramate or metallic salts, reacting with chemical hydrogen peroxide or bleach triggers heat buildup, severe shaft breakage, and greenish discoloration.
Phase 2

Temporary Coloration (Color Refresh)

Temporarily adjusts tone by adding surface reflections. Does not cover grey hair.

  • Mechanism: High-molecular-weight pigments (large color molecules) deposited via physical and electrostatic adsorption. REMOVAL: 1-2 washes.
  • Composition: Free of ammonia and oxidants; uses direct dyes (azo, anthraquinone).
Phase 3

Direct / Semi-Permanent Coloration

Partially covers greys and lasts 4-6 weeks (6-12 washes). Does not lighten.

  1. Penetration: Medium-sized molecules penetrate the outer cuticle/cortex at neutral or mildly acidic pH (5.5–7.0).
  2. Fixation: Retained by Van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonds (weak chemical interactions).
▼
Phase 4

Demi-Permanent Coloration

Deeper penetration into the cortex (lasts 24-28 washes). Uses ethanolamine (milder alkalizing agent than ammonia) and low-strength H2O2 (1.9% - 4%) (diluted hydrogen peroxide) at pH 7.5–8.5. Reduced concentration of precursors and couplers (resorcinol). Ammonia-free.
Phase 5

Permanent (Oxidative) Coloration

Permanent modification of color structure.
Two-Step Mechanism:
  1. Alkalinization (pH 9–10): Ammonia/MEA lifts cuticles. H2O2 irreversibly breaks down natural melanin.
  2. Chromogenesis: Precursors (PPD) + couplers (resorcinol) enter and assemble into large molecules (indamines) trapped inside the fiber.
A final acidifying post-treatment is required to seal cuticles.

CRITICAL INGREDIENTS and Restricted Substances (Reg. EC 1223/2009) 🛑

Reg. EC No. 1223/2009 (and subsequent updates) enforces strict restrictions or bans on potentially hazardous, carcinogenic, mutagenic, or endocrine-disrupting substances (EDCs).

MEA / TEA / DEADEA (Diethanolamine) and derivatives can react with nitrosating agents forming carcinogenic nitrosamines.DEA banned with nitrosating agents. Nitrosamine limit < 50 µg/kg.

Petrolatum & ParaffinsRisk of contamination by PAHs (Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons) (potentially toxic substances).Allowed only if fully refined with proven history according to European Pharmacopoeia.

HAIR SHAMPOO: Function and Composition 🧼

Shampoo is a complex aqueous colloidal system. Its primary function is the mechanical removal of sebum and dirt through the synergistic action of surfactants, without altering the physiological barrier of the scalp.

Formulation Matrix and Functional Roles

A standard formulation consists predominantly of deionized water (70-80%) as a universal solvent and a surfactant system (10-15%) responsible for cleansing. Critical functional components are added to ensure product stability and skin tolerance.

  • Surfactant System: A balanced blend of primary (cleansing) and secondary (mildness-enhancing) surfactants. (See subsequent table for chemical classification and charges).
  • Chelating Agents (Sequestrants): Molecules like EDTA or citrates are essential to bind calcium and magnesium ions present in hard water. Without them, surfactants would precipitate, reducing foam and leaving dull residues on the hair.
  • Buffer System (pH): Additives such as citric acid or lactic acid maintain the product at pH 4.5–5.5. This range is crucial to respect the scalp's acid mantle and keep the hair cuticles closed and shiny.
  • Rheology Modifiers: Salts (sodium chloride) or cellulosic polymers that increase the solution's viscosity, improving handling during application.
  • Preservative System: Necessary due to the high water content and presence of organic nutrients. Prevents microbial contamination (bacteria and molds) during product shelf life.
  • Conditioning Agents: Polymers or silicones that deposit a thin film onto the fiber. (The electrostatic deposition mechanism is covered in the following block).
  • Aesthetic Additives: Fragrances, colorants, and opacifying agents (e.g., glycol distearate) that provide the characteristic pearlescent appearance and scent, without directly influencing cleansing.

Surfactant Classes and Electrical Charge

TypeNet ChargeChemical ExampleFunctional Role
AnionicNegative (-)Sodium Laureth Sulfate (SLES), SLSPrimary cleansing and abundant foam. Can be harsh if unbuffered.
Amphoteric (Zwitterionic)Variable (pH-dependent)Cocamidopropyl BetaineMildness enhancers and foam stabilizers. At physiological pH (5.5), they reduce anionic irritation potential.
Non-IonicNeutral (0)Decyl Glucoside, AlkanolamidesUltra-mild cleansing, co-surfactants for sensitive skin. Excellent skin tolerance.
CationicPositive (+)Cetrimonium Chloride, PolyquaterniumConditioning and antistatic agents. Non-cleansing: they bind to negatively charged keratin.

Cleansing Mechanism (Micellar Dynamics)

Surfactants are amphiphilic molecules equipped with a hydrophobic (lipophilic) tail and a polar hydrophilic head. Dirt removal follows a well-defined sequential process:

Phase 1: Amphiphilic Alignment
Lipophilic Interaction
In an aqueous environment, the hydrophobic tails of surfactants orient towards sebum and lipid debris deposited on the hair fiber or scalp.
↓
Phase 2: CMC Threshold & Aggregation
Micelle Formation
Above the Critical Micelle Concentration (CMC), molecules self-assemble into spherical (or cylindrical/"worm-like") aggregates, enclosing dirt within the core.
↓
Phase 3: Mechanical Removal
Emulsification & Rinsing
The outer hydrophilic heads interact with rinse water, allowing full solubilization and removal of the hydrophobic micellar structure.

Treatment Shampoos (Anti-Dandruff and Anti-Seborrheic)

Special formulations containing active ingredients targeted to normalize cell turnover or counteract microbial proliferation (Malassezia spp.).

Anti-Dandruff (Antifungals and Cytostatics):
Utilize active ingredients permitted by EU Cosmetics Regulation such as Piroctone Olamine and Climbazole. Zinc Pyrithione is banned in the EU as a CMR 1B substance. In strictly pharmacological settings (OTC medicines or prescriptions), Ketoconazole or Selenium Disulfide are used instead.
Note: Coal tars are banned in the EU; vegetable oils (Cade, Birch) are used for their keratolytic and anti-itch properties.
Anti-Seborrheic:
  • Gentle Cleansers: Non-ionic or amphoteric surfactants (e.g., glucose derivatives) that cleanse without excessively stripping the hydrolipid film, preventing reactive seborrhea.
  • Sebum-Regulating Actives: Ingredients like Zinc PCA or plant extracts (e.g., Serenoa Repens) modulating 5-alpha-reductase activity to reduce sebum production.

Silicones in Cosmetics

Silicones (inorganic silicon-oxygen based polymers, e.g., Dimethicone, Cyclomethicone) form a breathable occlusive film on the hair surface. This reduces friction (improving combability), adds shine, and protects against humidity. They are chemically inert, hypoallergenic, and non-irritating.

The key distinction is between volatile (cyclic) and non-volatile (linear) silicones.
Regulation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1328 on restrictions of cyclic silicones D4, D5, and D6 in rinse-off products is fully in force. The measure targets their persistent and bioaccumulative (PBT/vPvB) environmental profile, not human health toxicity.
Comedogenicity: Modern silicones (e.g., high molecular weight Dimethicone) are generally non-comedogenic as their macromolecules are too large to obstruct hair follicles.

POST-SHAMPOO PRODUCTS: Conditioning and Chemico-Functional Treatment 🧴

1. Hair Conditioners

Formulations engineered to restore the tribological properties of the hair fiber, enhancing elasticity, cuticular smoothness, shine, and combability (reducing dynamic friction forces) and neutralizing surface static charges. Indicated for xerotic, chemically treated, or structurally damaged fibers.

  • Composition (Interfacial Phase): Linear chain fatty alcohols acting as co-emulsifiers and structuring agents (e.g., Cetearyl Alcohol), amphipathic cationic surfactants (long alkyl chain quaternary ammonium salts like Behentrimonium Chloride or Cetrimonium Chloride), high molecular weight silicone polymers (dimethicone and functionalized amodimethicone), synthetic emollient esters, low molecular weight hydrolyzed proteins (microencapsulated for stability and delivery), and substantive film-forming polymers.
  • Chemico-Physical Mechanism (Molecular Insight): Positive charges of the conditioner electrostatically bind to free anionic sites (ionized carboxyl groups COO- of aspartic and glutamic acid residues) of exposed keratin. The isoelectric point of keratin (pH ~ 3.7) is altered by alkaline treatments or washing, increasing negative charge density which this system saturates, promoting cuticle alignment and sealing.
  • Persistence and Kinetics: Predominantly reversible surface interaction; the conditioning film is subject to desorption and progressive kinetic removal via subsequent washes with anionic surfactants.
  • Dermatological Contraindications: If applied close to the follicular ostium or on seborrheic scalps, they can induce surface buildup (rinse-resistant deposition) and accelerate capillary migration of fluid sebum along the shaft.

2. Nutritive Hair Masks

Emulsified systems with high viscosity and pseudoplastic rheological consistency, formulated for topical post-shampoo applications with extended contact times (5-15 minutes). Aimed at structural restoration of the Cell Membrane Complex (cuticular CMC) and deep lipid replenishment of the outer hydrophobic layer.

Colloidal Structure: Predominantly oil-in-water (O/W) emulsions organized in liquid crystalline lamellar phases, stabilized by high-HLB ethoxylated non-ionic surfactants (polysorbates) or biodegradable ester-structured cationic surfactants (esterquats, like di-alkylester quaternary ammonium salts).

Over-conditioning Pathophysiology: Over-frequent application or inadequate rinsing saturates cuticular porosity, leading to rheological weighing down of the fiber, loss of natural volume, and early onset of surface oiliness through coalescence of applied lipids with endogenous sebum (greasy effect).

3. Styling Lotions

Topical leave-in formulations engineered to deposit onto the cuticle and create temporary inter-fiber bridges via synthetic homopolymeric or bio-based film-formers (e.g., PVP, VP/VA Copolymer, vinyl acetate derivatives, or modified polysaccharide polymers). They act by temporarily modifying structural rigidity and granting geometric shape memory to styling.
Chemico-Physical Note: Overdosing or rapid solvent evaporation alters polymeric film cohesion relative to the keratin substrate, causing flaking (microscopic fracturing of the film into visible white flakes, macroscopically mistakable for pityriasic desquamation).

4. Functional Leave-in Treatments

Hydroalcoholic, hydroglycolic solutions or leave-in microemulsions applied to the pilosebaceous unit or hair lengths, serving as vehicles for sustained release and transcutaneous absorption of target active ingredients.

Anti-Dandruff & Turnover
Antimicrobial Lotions
Ensure prolonged contact time for actives compliant with Reg. 1223/2009 (Piroctone Olamine against Malassezia furfur, Climbazole, and keratolytic Salicylic Acid). Formulated without Zinc Pyrithione (CMR 1B) to prevent skin hypersensitivity reactions.
Anti-Seborrheic & Sebum-Control
Lipogenesis Modulators
Reduce sebaceous synthesis at the ostium via Bioavailable Colloidal Sulfur, Azeloglycine (5-α-reductase inhibitor), lipophilic BHA, and astringent/soothing botanical extracts (Sage, Nettle, Aloe vera).
Anti-Hair Loss Coadjutants & Trichogenic Focus
Follicular Stimulation and DHT Blockade
Advanced systems to extend the Anagen phase and counteract androgenetic miniaturization. Utilize biomimetic peptide complexes, microcirculatory/VEGF stimulants (Caffeine, Nicotinates, Biotin), and local DHT inhibition by blocking the 5-α-reductase isoenzyme (e.g., phytosterols of Serenoa repens).
