PIGMENTATION DISORDERS (DYSCHROMIAS) 🔬

Melanin, synthesized by melanocytes (dendritic cells of the basal layer), is the biological pigment responsible for skin phototype. Dyschromias are qualitative or quantitative alterations of normal pigmentation, classified into hypochromias (pigment deficit) and hyperchromias (pigment excess).

Hyperchromias (Melanoderma)

These are divided into generalized forms (related to systemic diseases such as Addison's disease, hemochromatosis, or specific vitamin deficiencies) and localized forms.

Ephelides (Freckles):
  • Characteristics: Yellow-brown flat macules with blurred margins, typical of light phototypes (I-II).
  • Etiology: Induced by UV exposure; characterized by increased tyrosinase activity and melanosome volumetric index, without an increase in melanocyte count.
  • Course: Marked seasonal pattern (darken in summer and partially fade in winter). No neoplastic transformation potential.
Solar Lentigo (Actinic / Senile Lentigo):
  • Characteristics: Flat hyperpigmented macules with well-defined margins ("sharp borders"). Unlike ephelides, they persist stably year-round and express chronic photo-aging (cumulative actinic damage).
  • Histopathology: Linear and focal hyperplasia of melanocytes along the dermo-epidermal junction.
  • Treatment Approach: Targeted cryotherapy, laser therapy (Q-switched/Picosecond), or topical depigmenting agents.
Melanocytic Nevi (Acquired Nevus):

Benign melanocytic proliferation organized in nests of nevus cells. Classified by histological site into junctional (flat), compound (slightly raised), or dermal (tuberous/papillomatous). Dysplastic nevi (atypical) require strict clinical monitoring due to the risk of melanoma evolution or simulation.

Clinical Protocol: ABCDE Rule for Melanoma Screening

Dermoscopy

Clinical monitoring parameters:
• A - Asymmetry: Two halves of the lesion do not match.
• B - Borders: Irregular, notched, or poorly defined.
• C - Color: Variable, polychromatic (brown, black, red, white, blue).
• D - Diameter: Greater than 6 mm.
• E - Evolution: Rapid changes in size, shape, color, or symptoms.
Additional signs: spontaneous bleeding, localized itching, peri-lesional erythematous halo (Meyerson's sign).

Other Localized Hyperchromias:
Melasma (including chloasma gravidarum with hormonal etiology), actinic lentigo, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH), and hyperchromic manifestations of tinea versicolor.

Hypochromias (Leukodermas)

Clinical conditions characterized by a marked reduction or total absence of melanin synthesis.

Vitiligo:
  • Etiology: Chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by selective destruction of epidermal melanocytes, mediated by CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes, with strong genetic predisposition.
  • Clinical Picture: Milk-white achromic macules with sharp hyperpigmented borders, often symmetrically distributed. Leukotrichia (hair whitening within lesions) indicates involvement of the follicular melanocyte reservoir, a poor prognostic sign.
  • Management & Risks: Achromic skin lacks natural protection against ultraviolet (UV) radiation (high risk of sunburns and actinic carcinogenesis). Broad-spectrum topical sun protection (SPF 50+) is mandatory.
Oculocutaneous Albinism (OCA):
  • Etiology: Heterogeneous group of autosomal recessive genetic disorders characterized by total or partial absence of melanin synthesis. Melanocytes are present microscopically but dysfunctional due to congenital enzyme deficits (e.g., tyrosinase gene mutation in OCA1).
  • Clinical Picture: Achromic skin, white or straw-blonde hair, translucent blue-gray irides with red pupillary reflex on transillumination.
  • Ocular Complications: Foveal hypoplasia, congenital nystagmus, severe photophobia, strabismus, and impaired vision due to altered optic nerve fiber decussation at the chiasm.
Other Hypochromias:
Pityriasis alba (common in atopic dermatitis), post-infectious hypochromic tinea versicolor, nevus anemicus (congenital vascular adrenergic receptor defect), and idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis.

PRIMARY AND SECONDARY SKIN LESIONS: Classification & Diagnosis 🔬

Primary lesions represent the fundamental morphological unit of skin response to endogenous or exogenous insults. Dermatological diagnosis relies on systematic analysis of morphology, extent, configuration, and spatial distribution.

Onset / Healthy Skin
Primary Lesions
Direct primary manifestations of disease arising on previously healthy skin.
Examples: Macule, papule, plaque, nodule, wheal, vesicle, bulla, pustule.
Evolution / Traumatic Insult
Secondary Lesions
Natural evolution of primary lesions or results of physical/mechanical trauma.
Examples: Scale, crust, excoriation, erosion, ulceration, fissure, scar.
Polymorphic Coexistence
Primary-Secondary Patterns
Simultaneous presence of active primary lesions and evolving secondary lesions (e.g., Eczema/Dermatitis: erythema and vesicles coexisting with excoriations and lichenification).

Primary Lesions (Initial)

Vascodynamic
Erythema
Redness from superficial dermal plexus vasodilation. Positive dioscopy (blanches under pressure).
Examples: Infectious exanthems, sunburn, rosacea.
Pigmentary / Hemorrhagic
Macule / Patch
Non-palpable color change. Negative dioscopy. Hyperpigmented, hypopigmented, or hemorrhagic (purpura, petechiae).
Sizing: Macule (≤ 1 cm), Patch (> 1 cm).
Solid Superficial
Papule / Plaque
Elevated solid lesion. Papule (≤ 1 cm), Plaque (> 1 cm). Caused by epidermal hyperplasia or inflammatory infiltrate.
Examples: Lichen planus, psoriasis.
Solid Deep
Nodule / Nodosity
Nodule (> 1 cm, mid-deep dermis). Nodosity (deep dermo-hypodermal infiltrative process, e.g., erythema nodosum).
Edematous Transient
Wheal (Urtica)
Histamine-mediated acute papillary dermal edema. Transient (< 24h), accompanied by severe pruritus.
Examples: Urticaria, insect bites.
Serous / Purulent
Vesicle / Bulla / Pustule
Fluid collections: Vesicle (≤ 5 mm), Bulla (> 5 mm). Pustule (purulent exudate, septic or aseptic).

Secondary Lesions (Evolutive)

Hyperkeratosis
Scale
Visible accumulation of stratum corneum flakes (pityriasic, psoriasiform, lamellar). Sign of altered keratinization.
Exudate Drying
Crust
Dried serum, blood, or pus (serous, hemorrhagic, purulent). Temporarily replaces damaged epithelium.
Superficial (No Scar)
Excoriation / Erosion
Excoriation (traumatic/scratching, epidermis only). Erosion (pathological). Both heal without scarring.
Deep (With Scar)
Ulceration / Fissure
Ulceration (tissue loss extending into dermis/subcutis). Fissure (linear wall breakdown). Heal with permanent scarring.
Reproductive Repair
Scar (Cicatrix)
Newly formed collagenous fibrous tissue lacking skin appendages. Types: normotrophic, atrophic, hypertrophic, keloid.
Differential Diagnosis: Simple skin atrophy retains residual appendages, absent in true scars.

HAIR SHAFT ANOMALIES: STRUCTURAL FRACTURES & DEFORMITIES 💔

Hair shaft anomalies are structural defects compromising keratin fiber strength, classified by damage location (cuticle, cortex, medulla) and etiology (acquired/traumatic vs. genetic/congenital).

Acquired Fracture
1. Trichorrhexis Nodosa
Focal cuticle loss and cortical fraying. Whitish nodules with "brush-like" fractures.
Etiology: Cumulative physical-chemical trauma (heat, bleaching, perms).
Congenital / Sulfur Deficit
2. Trichodystrophy (Clean Break)
Clean transverse fracture. Polarized microscopy reveals a "tiger-tail" pattern.
Association: Sign of Trichothiodystrophy (TTD) due to cystine deficiency.
Pathognomonic
3. Trichorrhexis Invaginata (Bamboo Hair)
Intussusception deformity: distal segment invaginates into the proximal segment ("ball-and-socket" joint).
Association: Netherton Syndrome (SPINK5 mutation).
Mitotic Arrest
4. Pencil-Point Hair
Breakage upon rapid shaft thinning. Tapered proximal fragment.
Association: Alopecia Areata and chemotherapy-induced dystrophic anagen.
Physicochemical Degradation
5. Trichoptilosis (Split Ends)
Distal longitudinal splitting due to cuticle weathering.
Etiology: Exclusively acquired via mechanical or chemical trauma.
Incomplete Fracture
6. Trichoclasia (Greenstick)
Incomplete transverse fracture of cortex and medulla with intact cuticle bridging.
Etiology: Moderate physical trauma or mechanical bending.

SHAFT REGULARITY & STRUCTURAL DEFORMITIES 📏

Longitudinal or transverse shaft morphology defects. The key clinical distinction lies in regularity (often genetic) versus irregularity (often acquired or traumatic).

Regular Hereditary
1. Monilethrix (Beaded Hair)
Regular elliptical nodes alternating with thin internodes (breakage sites).
Etiology: Keratin gene mutations (KRT81, KRT83, KRT86) or Desmoglein 4 (DSG4).
Acquired Artifact
2. Pseudomonilethrix
Irregularly spaced widenings with intact cuticle.
Distinction: Traumatic/mechanical origin, non-hereditary.
Axial Torsion
3. Pili Torti (Twisted Hair)
Flattened shaft with 90°–180° torsions at irregular intervals. Sparkling reflection.
Association: Menkes Syndrome (ATP7A mutation, copper deficiency).
Mitotic Slowdown
4. Tapered Hairs
Progressive narrowing along shaft with intact cuticle.
Significance: Temporary follicular matrix inhibition (Alopecia Areata, trichotillomania).
Triangular Cross-Section
5. Longitudinal Grooves
Longitudinal groove and triangular cross-section.
Pathognomonic: Uncombable Hair Syndrome (UHS), spun-glass hair.
Air Bands
6. Pili Annulati (Ringed Hair)
Alternating light and dark bands due to cortical air cavities.
Clinical: Hereditary (locus 12q). Non-fragile; purely cosmetic.
Partial Duplication
7. Pili Bifurcati
Shaft splits into two distinct branches, each with its own cuticle.
Mechanism: Temporary secondary matrix or papilla duplication.
Shared Ostium
8. Pili Multigemini
2–10 distinct shafts emerging from a single follicular ostium.
Differential: Distinct from Trichostasis Spinulosa (retained telogen hairs).

RESIDUAL ANOMALIES AND HAIR SHAFT CURVATURE ALTERATIONS ➰

This section groups acquired defects resulting from mechanical trauma (knotting) and congenital anomalies that alter the transverse geometry or curvature of the hair shaft, affecting combability and cosmetic appearance without necessarily causing structural fracture fragility.

1. Trichonodosis (Knotted Hair / Trichonodosis)

Definition:
An exclusively acquired anomaly characterized by the formation of genuine knots along the hair shaft (single-strand knots). At the knot loop, mechanical stress induces cuticle scaling, exposing and fraying the underlying cortex.
Pathogenesis and Biomechanics:
Results from repeated mechanical trauma (aggressive brushing, friction). A highly flattened or elliptical cross-section reduces the torsional moment of inertia (i.e., the structural resistance of the shaft to twisting upon itself), promoting self-curling and knotting (the "spring effect").
Risk Factors:
Prevalent in individuals with curly, kinky, or fine hair (African ethnicity or curly Caucasian hair). Rarely spontaneous in extremely long, neglected hair.

2. Uncombable Hair Syndrome (Pili Trianguli et Canaliculi - UHS)

Pediatric clinical condition linked to the microscopic hallmark of Pili trianguli et canaliculi (triangular shaft cross-section with longitudinal grooving), showing gradual spontaneous resolution during puberty.

Molecular Etiology and UHS Biochemical Cascade

Genetic Pathway

Genetic disorder with autosomal recessive inheritance linked to mutations in the follicular keratinization complex: PADI3, TGM3, TCHH, and SULT2B1.

Phase 1: Trichohyalin Deimination
PADI3 → TCHH
Peptidylarginine deiminase 3 (PADI3) deiminates trichohyalin (TCHH), enabling its cross-linking with keratin intermediate filaments.
↓
Phase 2: Isopeptide Cross-Linking
TGM3 (Transglutaminase 3)
Catalyzes stable isopeptide cross-links essential for structural consolidation.
↓
Pathological Outcome
Premature IRS Keratinization
Axis impairment leads to premature keratinization of the inner root sheath (IRS), exerting a deforming and rigidifying effect on the malleable shaft.

Clinical Correlate: Dry, unruly hair projecting outward, impossible to comb flat, yet devoid of significant loss in tensile strength.

3. Woolly Hair

Morphology and Differential Diagnosis:
Shafts displaying ovoid/flattened cross-sections with tight axial twists and irregular curvatures. Compared to Pili Torti (180° twists along the longitudinal axis), the twists are less structured and mechanical resistance is largely preserved.
Pathophysiology:
Marked reduction in the anagen phase (active growth phase, maximum hair length often < 5 cm). Incombability stems from the spatial density of micro-curvatures rather than shaft breakage.
Clinical VariantInheritance & GeneticsPathological Features & Associations
Hereditary (Generalized)Autosomal Dominant or RecessiveInvolves the entire scalp. Recessive forms serve as markers for severe cardio-cutaneous syndromes (e.g., Naxos disease or Carvajal syndrome due to mutations in desmosomal genes JUP or DSP).
Localized (Woolly Hair Nevus)Non-hereditaryCircumscribed patch on a healthy scalp; occasionally present in mosaicism associated with epidermal nevi.
Acquired (Induced Kinky Hair)Iatrogenic / ReactiveRare, secondary to systemic drugs (systemic retinoids such as acitretin/isotretinoin, EGFR inhibitors) or early-stage androgenetic alopecia.

SEBORRHEA AND SEBACEOUS DYSFUNCTION 💧

Seborrhea is defined as a quantitative increase in sebum production (seborrhea oleosa) or a qualitative alteration in its lipid composition (seborrhea sicca). Rather than a standalone pathology, it represents a homeostatic dysfunction that impairs the surface hydrolipid film, establishing a microenvironment permissive to acne, dandruff, and seborrheic dermatitis.

Clinical Classification of Seborrhea

Clinical FormPathophysiological MechanismCutaneous Manifestations & Consequences
Physiological SeborrheaBalanced holocrine secretory activity regulated by age, sex, endocrine status, and genetics.Maintenance of the hydrolipid barrier and physiological shaft lubrication.
Pathological Seborrhea (Oleosa)Quantitative hyperproduction of sebum.Hyper-oily skin and appendages, sebaceous retention (oxidized sebum stasis), comedones, and dysbiosis of the cutaneous microbiota.
Seborrhea SiccaQualitative alteration of the lipid fraction: linoleic acid depletion alongside squalene hydroperoxide excess.Desquamative and xerotic appearance (pathological skin dryness), despite normal or elevated gland secretion rates.

Pathophysiology and Molecular Mechanisms

Molecular Cascade of Seborrhea

Endocrinology & Microbiome
Endocrine Stimulus
Testosterone → DHT
Synthesis of 5α-dihydrotestosterone via type I 5α-reductase. DHT binds to the androgen receptor (AR).
Signaling Potentiation
IGF-1 / Insulin
Activation of the mTORC1 axis, amplifying and co-stimulating the lipogenic pathway.
↓
Gene Activation
SREBP-1c Pathway
Transcription of Sterol Regulatory Element-Binding Protein, directly triggering lipogenesis in sebocytes.
Lipid Alteration & Peroxidation:
Depletion of linoleic acid (vital for barrier function and inter-keratinocyte cohesion) accompanied by a relative increase in squalene. Peroxidized squalene (squalene monohydroperoxide) triggers a pro-inflammatory state and infundibular hyperkeratosis (follicular ostium thickening).
Role of Microbiota and Malassezia spp.:
Opportunistic lipophilic yeasts Malassezia restricta and M. globosa metabolize sebaceous triglycerides via extracellular lipases, releasing irritant free fatty acids (e.g., oleic acid). Subsequent penetration into the stratum corneum leads to inflammation, pruritus, and reactive desquamation.

Clinical Consequences and Differential Diagnosis

  • Androgenetic Alopecia: Seborrhea acts as a cofactor: perifollicular microinflammation accelerated by lipid peroxides and microbiota exacerbates the miniaturization of susceptible follicles.
  • Folliculitis and Acne Vulgaris: Microcomedone occlusion creates an anoxic environment suited for Cutibacterium acnes hyperproliferation, unleashing an inflammatory cascade.
  • Pityriasis Steatoides: Intermediate condition characterized by yellowish, greasy scales adhering to the scalp, soaked in degraded sebum.
  • Seborrheic Dermatitis: Chronic relapsing dermatitis (erythema, scaling, and pruritus) concentrated in high-sebaceous-density zones, driven by complex interactions between sebum, Malassezia, and host immune response.

Therapeutic Approach and Sebum Regulation

Clinical management aims to reduce microbial load, normalize epidermal turnover, and modulate lipogenesis while preserving skin barrier integrity to prevent rebound hypersecretion.

Therapeutic ClassActive IngredientsClinical Mechanism of Action
Antifungals & AntimicrobialsKetoconazole / Ciclopirox Olamine
Piroctone Olamina / Zinc Pyrithione		Broad-spectrum activity against Malassezia spp.; cytostatic action (cell proliferation blockade) and microbiota normalization.
Keratolytics & Sebo-ModulatorsSalicylic Acid / Azelaic Acid
Zinc PCA / Niacinamide		Lipophilic keratolytic action (comedone plug clearing), anti-inflammatory effect, 5α-reductase inhibition, and protection against squalene peroxidation.
Physiotherapeutic & Instrumental SupportHigh Frequency
LLLT (Photobiomodulation)		Ozone generation exerting bactericidal, fungicidal, and vasomodulating effects; Low-Level Laser Therapy (LLLT) to mitigate inflammation and promote tissue repair.

DANDRUFF (PITYRIASIS SIMPLEX CAPITIS) 🌨️

Dandruff is a chronic non-inflammatory (or mildly inflammatory) disorder featuring visible desquamation of the scalp. It is driven by an accelerated epidermal turnover rate: keratinocyte transit time is reduced from ~28 days down to 2–7 days. Cells fail to achieve complete differentiation, aggregating into visible flakes before shedding.

Pathophysiology: Etiological Triad and Barrier Disruption

Etiopathogenetic Triad of Dandruff

Barrier Homeostasis
1. Sebum Excess (Substrate) + 2. Malassezia Colonization + 3. Individual Susceptibility
Pathogenesis mandates simultaneous interaction among all three parameters (genetics, immune profile, and barrier integrity).
Role of Malassezia:
Dandruff requires the presence of lipophilic Malassezia yeasts (specifically M. globosa and M. restricta). Bacterial and fungal lipases hydrolyze sebum triglycerides, liberating free fatty acids (e.g., oleic acid). In susceptible individuals, oleic acid penetrates the stratum corneum, instigating irritation, subclinical inflammation, and parakeratosis (nucleated keratinocyte retention in the stratum corneum due to hyperproliferation).
Skin Barrier Disruption:
Dandruff-affected stratum corneum displays a compromised barrier function and elevated permeability (increased TEWL — Transepidermal Water Loss). This facilitates irritant penetration and transepidermal water loss, sustaining a vicious cycle of dryness and flaking.

Clinical Classification of Dandruff

VariantScale MorphologyUnderlying Scalp ConditionClinical Context
Pityriasis Sicca (Dry Dandruff)Fine, white-to-grayish, powdery, loosely attached scales.Normal or mildly xerotic (dry). Pruritus minimal or absent.Commonly exacerbated during winter (low relative ambient humidity).
Pityriasis Steatoides (Greasy Dandruff)Large, oily, yellowish scales forming adherent plaques.Erythematous (reddened), oily, and inflamed.Represents a mild variant of seborrheic dermatitis; warrants targeted therapeutic management.

Therapeutic Strategy and Management

Therapeutic goals center on controlling Malassezia populations, restoring physiological epidermal differentiation rates, alleviating inflammation, and re-establishing barrier function.

Pharmacological CategoryActive IngredientsSpecific Mechanism of Action
Antifungal Agents• Ketoconazole (2%)
• Zinc Pyrithione (ZPT)
• Ciclopirox Olamine / Selenium Sulfide		Inhibition of ergosterol synthesis (fungal membrane integrity); fungicidal, antibacterial, and cytostatic activity to suppress keratinocyte hyperproliferation.
Keratolytic Agents• Salicylic Acid
• Sulfur		Promote chemical desquamation (corneocyte desquamation) and follicular penetration; exhibit sebostatic action. Lack direct antifungal properties.
Natural Adjuvants• Tea Tree Oil (Melaleuca alternifolia)Demonstrated antifungal efficacy in clinical trials targeting Malassezia species.

Correct Usage and Physicochemical Parameters

Usage Protocol

Formulations must maintain an acidic pH (4.0–5.5) to preserve the physiological acid mantle and create an unfavorable habitat for fungal proliferation (which thrives under neutral or alkaline pH conditions).

Contact time is critical: therapeutic shampoos require a 3–5 minute dwell time prior to rinsing. Clinical evidence confirms that exposure under 2 minutes significantly reduces antifungal and cytostatic efficacy.

HAIR: HOW IT IS MADE AND ITS LIFE CYCLE

1. ANATOMY AND STRUCTURE OF THE HAIR

Body hair and head hair are filaments made of keratin. They originate from a "sac" in the skin called the HAIR FOLLICLE.

The follicle is located beneath the skin of the scalp (dermis). Its concave end is called the BULB.

The length, thickness, and distribution of hair vary based on location, sex, age, and ethnicity.

Parts of the Hair

  • The part that emerges from the skin is called the SHAFT (or STEM).
  • The part under the skin (inside the follicle) is called the ROOT.
  • At the bottom of the root lies the DERMAL PAPILLA. This papilla delivers nutrients to the hair.
  • Between the bulb and the root is the HAIR MATRIX. The matrix produces all the components of the hair.

These parts form the PILOSEBACEOUS UNIT.

PILOSEBACEOUS UNIT: COMPONENTS

  • ▶ HAIR FOLLICLE (with hair)
  • ▶ ARRECTOR PILI MUSCLE
  • ▶ SEBACEOUS GLAND

HAIR FOLLICLE:

The follicle is an inclined "sac" in the skin that extends 1-3 mm into the dermis. It contains the hair and its sheaths.

Each person has about 5 million follicles. Around 100,000 are on the scalp. This number is set before birth and does not increase.

SEBACEOUS GLAND:

This gland produces sebum, a fatty substance (triglycerides, cholesterol, etc.).

Sebum serves to lubricate, soften, and protect the hair as it grows. It spreads over the skin and hair. Its activity is regulated by hormonal and dietary factors.

ARRECTOR PILI MUSCLE:

It is composed of smooth muscle fibers attached to the follicle.

When it contracts (due to cold or emotions like fear), the hair stands upright, causing goosebumps. It also helps push sebum out.

2. STRUCTURE OF THE HAIR

Hair is a complex fiber containing water (10-30%) and lipids (sebum, waxes, etc.) for protection.

The hair shaft consists of three layers:

  • CUTICLE: The outermost layer. It is made of flat, overlapping cells, like roof tiles.
  • CORTEX: Located beneath the cuticle, it is the largest part of the hair. It provides strength and contains melanin (pigment).
  • MEDULLA: The central core, often absent in fine hair.

The main components are: keratin (structure), melanin (color), and minerals.

KERATIN: THE FUNDAMENTAL STRUCTURE

Hair is primarily made of keratin, present in two forms:

  • Filamentous Keratin: Forms bundles (fibrils) in the cortex.
  • Amorphous Keratin: Fills the spaces between bundles, providing stability.

HOW IS STRUCTURAL STABILITY MAINTAINED?

Keratin chains are held together by "bonds". There are 3 types of bonds:

1. HYDROGEN BONDS

These are very weak bonds that break easily with water or heat, providing flexibility.

2. SALT BONDS

These are moderately strong bonds broken by high heat or acidic/basic conditions, providing strength.

3. DISULFIDE BONDS

These are very strong covalent bonds formed by sulfur atoms.

They determine structure (e.g., naturally curly hair) and can only be broken with significant chemical energy.

All three bond types contribute to overall hair resistance.

MINERALS

Minerals are essential. A deficiency makes hair fragile, dry, and dull.

Key minerals include:

  • IRON: Deficiency causes brittleness and excessive shedding.
  • COPPER: Essential for pigment production (melanin) and disulfide bonds.
  • ZINC: Crucial for cellular growth and repair.

LIPIDS (FATS)

Lipids mainly originate from sebum.

Phospholipids are key to maintaining proper hair hydration.

MELANIN: NATURAL COLOR

Melanin is the natural pigment found in the cortex, produced by melanocytes.

Types of pigment:

  • EUMELANIN: Provides brown/black tones (dark hair).
  • PHEOMELANIN: Provides yellow/red tones (blond and red hair).
  • TRICHOCHROMES: Special pigments responsible for vibrant red shades.

Melanin is synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine. The ratio of these pigments determines final hair color.

3. HAIR LIFE CYCLE

Hair goes through repeated growth and resting phases. When an old hair falls out, the follicle generates a new one.

The cycle consists of 3 phases:

1. ANAGEN: Growth phase

The longest phase. The hair matrix is highly active, driving continuous growth.

  • Duration: 2-4 years in men, 3-7 years in women.
  • Hair grows approximately 1-1.5 cm per month.

2. CATAGEN: Transition phase

A very short phase lasting 2-4 weeks, during which growth stops.

3. TELOGEN: Resting phase

The resting period, lasting around 3 months.

The old hair sheds only when pushed out by new emerging hair.

Human hair shedding follows a mosaic pattern: each follicle operates independently, preventing widespread hair loss at once.

Note: Each follicle can undergo up to 30 life cycles.
